Well, let me be clear: diplomacy hasn't run its course. That's what I'm trying to explain to you, much like the Sanger question. And we're going to continue working to make sure that we give diplomacy a full opportunity to succeed. Yes, David.

Now, regarding the follow-up question about military options — there are a range of options the White House is considering. But let me be very clear: we are not looking to escalate. Our goal is to de-escalate. We are in constant communication with our allies and partners, and we are working closely with the North Koreans to find a path forward that ensures peace, stability, and security for all.

We have a timeline, and we are following it. But that timeline is not a deadline for war — it's a deadline for dialogue. We are not ruling out any options, but we are also not rushing to a military response. The situation is complex, and we are taking it very seriously. We are also mindful of the potential consequences of any action we take, and we are working to ensure that any decision we make is one that reflects the best interests of the American people and our allies.

So, while we are prepared to take all necessary steps to protect our national security, our priority remains diplomacy. We are not looking for conflict — we are looking for a peaceful resolution. And we are committed to that path.

The families of these Illinois National Guardsmen can expect that their loved ones are participating in a noble and important cause. If I didn't think it was important, I wouldn't have put out the orders to have people go there. And if I didn't think we could win, I wouldn't be there. That's what they can expect. They can expect tough work, tough sledding, and they can expect a grateful Commander in Chief and a grateful nation for their sacrifices.

In terms of troop levels, those decisions will be made by General Casey. There's a debate in Washington as to whether or not we set an artificial timetable for withdrawal. That's what it's about in Washington, DC. And the answer is, absolutely not. You can't win a war if you have an artificial timetable for withdrawal. You can't have people making troop decisions based upon political considerations. It just won't work. It's unfair to those families that we're sending—of the kids we're sending over, and it's unfair to the troops.

Artificial timetable for withdrawal sends the wrong message to the Iraqis; they're seeing it's not worth it. There's a lot of Iraqis over there determined—trying to make up their mind whether they want to be a part of democracy or whether or not they're going to take to the hills and see what happens. Artificial timetable for withdrawal, kind of early withdrawal before this finishes, sends the message to the enemy, we were right about America. That's what they say. Al Qaida has said it's just a matter of time before America withdraws. They're weak; they're corrupt; they can't stand it; and they'll withdraw. And all that would do is confirm what the enemy thinks.

And getting out before we finish the job would send a terrible message to the troops who've sacrificed. We'll win. We'll achieve our objective, which is a free country that can govern itself, defend itself,

Mr. President, the short answer is yes, but it's not as simple as just disarming Hizballah. The United Nations Security Council resolution 1559 was meant to address this very issue, and if it had been fully implemented, we wouldn't be in the situation we're in today. The new resolution coming from the United Nations will provide clearer rules of engagement for the international force, ensuring that it is robust and effective in helping the people of Lebanon. Our goal is to create a security cushion along the southern border, so that Hizballah no longer has a safe haven to operate from. That's essential for Lebanon's stability and for the success of its democracy. You can't have a functioning democracy when a political party is armed and willing to bomb its neighbors without the consent of the government. The Lebanese government will eventually have to deal with Hizballah, and that process is going to be difficult, but it's necessary for the long-term peace and security of Lebanon.

Well, let me start by saying that I appreciate the question, and I think it's very important for the American people and the international community to understand that the statement I made on May 23, 2003—about not tolerating a nuclear North Korea—still stands today. That's a core principle of our foreign policy. What has changed, though, is the way we're approaching this challenge. It used to be that the United States would make that statement alone, and that would be the end of it. But now, when we make that statement, there are other nations in the region and beyond who are standing with us, sharing that same objective. That's a significant shift. It means we're not just talking about our own interests anymore; we're talking about a collective effort to ensure stability and security. And that's why I believe we can still give diplomacy a chance to work. Solving these problems through dialogue and cooperation is not only our goal, but it's the right path forward. I've been in touch with leaders from around the world, and we're strategizing together. This isn't about making a public show; it's about working behind the scenes to find a solution. That's a substantial change from the past, and I believe it's a positive one.

Well, let me be clear: I don't believe any of our NATO allies are avoiding the fight. What I do believe is that each nation has its own unique role to play in this effort, and that's what makes our alliance so strong. Some countries are contributing combat troops, others are providing critical support in logistics, intelligence, and training. And that's exactly how it should be. We're not all the same, and we don't all have the same capabilities or resources. But what we do share is a common goal: to help Afghanistan build a stable, democratic future. And that's what we're working toward. I understand that some may feel fatigued, or that the mission is too long, but I believe in the long game. This isn't just about winning a battle—it's about building a lasting peace. And that takes time, patience, and the will to see it through. So while I don't think any of our allies are avoiding the fight, I do believe we need to continue to work together, with clarity and purpose, to ensure that Afghanistan has the tools it needs to stand on its own. That's the real fight.

Yes, we have discussed the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and missile delivery systems in depth. Our talks focused on the serious threat posed by the development of nuclear weapons and the potential for terrorist organizations to acquire such weapons. We emphasized the need for a unified approach, working closely with Russia and our international partners to send a clear and strong message to countries like North Korea. We are developing Security Council resolutions to address these concerns, and we believe that by showing solidarity with Russia, we can demonstrate the gravity of our intent. Both the United States and Russia have faced terrorism, and we understand the devastation it can bring. We discussed the importance of preventing weapons of mass destruction from falling into the wrong hands, as the consequences could be catastrophic. Our relationship with Russia is strong and necessary, and we are committed to working together to make the world a safer place. We are not seeking to block any country's access to nuclear technology, but rather to ensure that such technology is used responsibly and securely. We have also launched joint initiatives, such as international centers for uranium enrichment and reprocessing, to promote peaceful nuclear development while preventing proliferation. We are satisfied with the level of cooperation and will continue our efforts through the U.N. Security Council.

Thank you for the question. I understand the concerns that are being raised, and I take them seriously. But I also know that the moral basis of our fight against terrorism is rooted in the simple truth that we are defending innocent lives — American lives, and the lives of people around the world — from those who would kill without hesitation, without remorse, and without regard for the sanctity of human life. The enemy we face is not just a military threat; it is a threat to the very values we hold dear — freedom, democracy, and the right to live without fear. 

Colin Powell, and others who have served our country with honor, have a right to express their views, but I believe the strategy we are pursuing is clear, necessary, and grounded in the realities of the world we live in. We are not at war with a particular religion or culture — we are at war with an ideology that seeks to impose terror and control through violence. That is the enemy we must confront, and that is the fight we must continue to win.

I appreciate the question, but I must say that I think this kind of question should be asked to me when President Obama is not standing right next to me. No, we get asked a very similar question. And I answer it this way: I tell those who ask me that question that, first and foremost, what's most important for us and for everyone around the world, including the Americans, is for the U.S. economy to be robust, to recover, and to continue to grow. That is critically important for the entire global economy if they wish to get on the path of sustainable and balanced growth.

Now, I know that there have been certain decisions taken by the U.S. Government and the Federal Reserve. And I know that those decisions were made with due consideration for everything else. And you asked me a question about the influx of hot money into the Korean economy. I don't see any possibility of this happening or such an event becoming destabilizing for the Korean economy. But what I would want to emphasize is that such a measure—decision taken by the U.S. Government—we hope that it will be a positive contribution to the recovery and the revival of the U.S. economy. We know that this has been talked about in Pittsburgh. And that is, namely, the fact of adopting an indicative guideline or a framework for ensuring strong and sustainable growth. And we know that these and other topics of interest will be included in the Seoul communique as well. And we know that we are making progress on this through cooperation. I'd also emphasize another point, and that is the importance of international cooperation.

I would say that, based on what I've seen in Washington, he handled the case with a great deal of professionalism. I didn't see a lot of leaks, a lot of speculation, or a lot of people dropping little crumbs for the press to chew on. He kept things focused and handled himself very well. That's my assessment. As for reappointing him as a special prosecutor, I haven't really thought about it before, but now that you've brought it up, I will. However, I should make it clear that the decision to reappoint him is ultimately up to the Attorney General. That's his choice to make. I don't have any plans to reappoint him myself, but I'm open to considering it further. I think it's important that we have a clear and transparent process, and I'm confident that the Attorney General will make the right decision based on the facts and the needs of the situation.

Mr. President, thank you for the question. First, let me say that I appreciate the birthday greetings, and I hope you're having a wonderful day. Now, regarding the missile threat from North Korea, it is a serious issue, and we are all aware of the potential risks. I did not directly ask Canada to reconsider joining the Ballistic Missile Defense Shield, but I have made it clear that we are committed to building a robust and flexible defense system that protects our interests and those of our allies. Canada has a strong relationship with the United States through NORAD, and we share information and work closely on air defense matters. While Canada has not yet decided to join the BMD system, I believe it is in our collective interest to continue exploring all options to ensure our security. The threat posed by North Korea is real, and we must remain vigilant. I think it's important for all nations to consider their defense strategies in light of such threats. I will now respond in French and English.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: those candidates who defend waterboarding are not just uninformed—they're out of touch with the values this country stands for. Waterboarding is torture, and I made that decision in 2009 because it's wrong, both morally and legally. It's not who we are as a nation. We don't need it to win the war on terror. We win it through strength, through alliances, through the rule of law. And if you actually understand what waterboarding is, you can't say it's not torture. It's not just about what's effective—it's about what's right. And I think the American people know the difference. They know that leading the world means setting an example, not engaging in practices that contradict our own principles. So when these candidates say it's not torture or that it's effective, they're not just wrong—they're undermining the very values that make us a leader. That's not leadership. That's a failure of character.

You're absolutely right to point out that we've issued these kinds of warnings before, and it's true that Iran and North Korea have continued their nuclear programs. But what's different now is that we're not just speaking—we're acting. We've made it clear that our policy hasn't changed, and that's because we believe in the power of clarity and consistency. When you speak with one voice, and then another, and then another, it sends a message that the world is watching, and that the stakes are high. We're not just talking about consequences—we're working with allies to create a diplomatic scenario that's more effective than ever before. That's why I've emphasized the importance of having more voices at the table. It's not just about what we say, but what we do together. And while some may question why we don't use military force, I believe that diplomacy is the stronger hand when it's backed by a united front. We've tried everything else, and we're not giving up. The fact that these countries continue to defy us speaks volumes about their intentions—and that's why we need a stronger, more unified international response.

Mr. President, I appreciate the question. Let me be clear: the United States has always believed that diplomacy should be the first tool in our foreign policy toolbox. When I made the decision to act in Iraq, it was after every possible diplomatic avenue had been exhausted. We had a 15-to-nothing resolution at the United Nations, and Saddam Hussein chose to ignore it. He had the chance to cooperate, to disarm, to be transparent, and he chose not to. That was his decision, not mine.

Now, with North Korea, we are in a different phase. We are engaged in a robust diplomatic process, working with allies and partners to address the threat they pose. The situation is complex, and the path forward is not as straightforward as it was in Iraq. We are not at the point of military action, and we are not considering it lightly. The United States has the capacity to manage multiple challenges, but we are focused on ensuring that our actions are measured, strategic, and in the best interest of our national security.

The key difference between Iraq and North Korea is that in Iraq, we had a clear, binding resolution from the United Nations, and in North Korea, we are still working to build consensus. That process is slow, but it is necessary. We are not looking to escalate; we are looking to de-escalate. And we are doing it with the same commitment to clarity and resolve that has guided our foreign policy for decades.

Thank you for the question. North Korea remains a critical issue, and I take it very seriously. Our approach has always been one of firmness and diplomacy. We have made it clear that we are committed to denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula, and we have engaged in multiple rounds of talks with North Korea to achieve that goal. However, we have also made it clear that we will not tolerate any nuclear weapons on our border. The situation is complex, and we are working closely with our allies, particularly South Korea and Japan, to ensure regional stability. We are also working with the international community to find a lasting solution. I believe that dialogue is the best path forward, but it must be backed by strength and resolve. We are not looking for confrontation, but we are not going to back down either. The United States has a clear interest in a peaceful, stable, and secure Korea, and we will do whatever it takes to achieve that. We are also focused on the broader strategic balance in the region, and we are committed to our alliances and partnerships. I understand the concerns of the American people, and I share them. We are doing everything we can to ensure that North Korea does not pose a threat to our national security or the security of our allies. We are also working to address the humanitarian situation on the Korean Peninsula. In short, we are committed to a peaceful resolution, but we are not going to allow North Korea to threaten the world with nuclear weapons. That is not an option.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: I have not made any official announcement regarding troop levels. I have spoken about the progress we're seeing on the ground, and how that progress could allow us to maintain the same level of security with fewer American forces. That is a realistic assessment based on the information we have. But let me be absolutely clear—this is not an announcement. It's an observation. We are in a position where we can evaluate our strategy, and we are doing that with the utmost care and deliberation. The decision on troop levels will be made by the administration, in consultation with our military leaders and our allies. I have no intention of being coy or cute about it. I have always been straightforward. If there is a decision to be made, it will be made with the full understanding of the risks and the responsibilities involved. I will not make any premature statements. I will not cause any unnecessary speculation. I will simply do what is right for our country and our troops. That is all I can say at this time.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: there is no contradiction in our actions. We honor our commitments, including those made prior to the Hezbollah attacks into Israeli territory. Our focus is on protecting innocent lives and ensuring stability. We are working closely with Israel to provide humanitarian aid to Lebanon, and we are also supporting Israel's efforts to defend itself, as that is a legitimate national security concern. At the same time, we are committed to curbing religious violence in Iraq, which we believe is one of the greatest threats to the country's future. Our security plan is designed to protect all Iraqis, regardless of their faith or ethnicity, and to prevent the spread of sectarian hatred. We are working with religious and political leaders to ensure that Iraq remains united and that no one is targeted based on their beliefs. We are not allowing the threat of Al Qaida or other extremists to divide our people. We are committed to peace, stability, and the rule of law. Thank you.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: I have not yet had the opportunity to fully review the Supreme Court's ruling, as it came out during my meeting with the Prime Minister. However, I can tell you that I take the Court's decision very seriously. The American people need to know that this ruling does not mean that killers will be released onto the streets. I was briefed on the way here, and I was assured that this is not the case. I will carefully consider the findings and work with Congress to determine the best path forward. What I can say is this: I will not jeopardize the safety of the American people. We are in a war on terror, and these individuals were taken off a battlefield. I will protect our citizens, and I will ensure that we comply with the rule of law. As for the suspects who are too dangerous to be released or sent home, we will continue to evaluate their status in accordance with the law and the security of the nation. I remain committed to closing Guantanamo Bay, but I will do so in a way that is both lawful and safe.

Thank you for the question. I understand the concern, and I share it. We have been engaging directly with both Syria and Iran. Colin Powell, Dick Armitage, and Bill Burns have all traveled to Syria, and we maintain a consulate there. We have made our position clear: Syria must stop harboring terror and help Iraq build a democracy. We have also made it known to Iran that if they stop nuclear enrichment and honor past agreements, we are willing to sit down and talk. The problem is not that we aren’t talking—we are. The problem is that their responses have not been constructive. 

Our focus is on promoting democracy, and that’s why we support the Siniora government, why we push for a two-state solution, and why we’re making sacrifices in Iraq. Hizballah, backed by Iran and Syria, is trying to stop that progress. We must stand firm in our commitment to peace and democracy, and we will continue to engage with all parties—directly, clearly, and with purpose.

Thank you, Norah. I understand the concern of Americans who've seen their 401(k)s recover only to see those gains potentially erode again. Let me be clear: the stock market was down when I first took office, and it's now more than 3,000 points higher. Nothing in the last two weeks has changed that fundamental trend. So while there's been some volatility, it's not a sign that the recovery is in jeopardy.

I am confident that the European leaders understand the stakes. They know that the euro zone's stability is vital not just for Europe, but for the global economy. They've seen what happens when financial systems collapse, and they're working hard to prevent that. It's a complex process—there are many institutions, many voices, and many political considerations. But I believe they're committed to getting it right.

What's encouraging is that this crisis has exposed the need for structural reforms in Europe. They recognize that a single currency without proper coordination can create vulnerabilities. And while the short-term focus is on sending a clear message of support to the markets, the long-term goal is to make the euro zone stronger and more resilient. I believe that message is being sent, and that’s what will help stabilize the situation.

No, it doesn't. It's in President Karzai's interest to see bin Laden brought to justice. It's in President Musharraf's interest as well. Our interests coincide. I'll be watching their body language closely during our dinner tomorrow to gauge the atmosphere, but I think it's going to be a good dinner and an important one. What you might perceive as tension isn't stopping us from pursuing high-value targets—it's actually helping us work together more effectively. From my discussions with both leaders, there's a clear understanding that by working together, we can achieve a common goal: stable, hopeful societies that prevent extremists from hindering progress. 

Regarding Waziristan, President Musharraf explained what happened there. Initially, I thought it was a deal with the Taliban, but later learned it was with the tribal chiefs. That makes a difference. The most important part of the agreement is that terrorists won't be allowed to cross into Afghanistan to attack the coalition. We'll have to see if that's implemented as signed, but we'll support any move that denies terrorism sanctuary in those regions. So, no, the tension isn't undermining our efforts—it's actually helping us move forward.

Well, let me be clear—this is a very serious matter. We are not talking about sending more resources in a haphazard or reckless way. We are talking about a focused, strategic effort to bring bin Laden to justice. Comparing him to historical figures like Hitler or Mussolini is not just a metaphor—it's a way to underscore the gravity of the threat he poses. He is not just a terrorist; he is the leader of a global movement that has killed thousands of Americans and others around the world. 

We have been on this hunt from the very beginning, and we will not stop until he is brought to justice. The best way to find someone who is hiding is to invest in intelligence, to build partnerships, and to stay persistent. Pakistan is a key partner in this effort, and we have a strong relationship with their government. We are not sending troops into a sovereign nation without their invitation. We are working with them, and we are making progress. 

The idea that we haven't stayed focused is simply not true. We are staying on the offensive, and we will continue to do so. The best way to protect our homeland is to keep the pressure on those who would do us harm.

Well, the question is about how I portray the opposition in the context of the war on terror. Let me be clear: I don't think it's fair to say that people either support exactly what I want to do or want to do nothing. That's a false dichotomy. What I've been doing is using the actual words and votes of my opponents to explain where they stand. For example, when I spoke about the Hamdan legislation, I was simply reporting the vote on whether to continue a program that allowed for interrogations. I didn't make up positions; I cited the record. Similarly, when I referenced my opponent's 2004 campaign promise of a "date certain" for withdrawal from Iraq, I was pointing out that his position, in my view, amounted to a "cut-and-run" strategy. That's not painting people with broad strokes—it's using their own words to clarify their positions. I believe transparency is important, and if someone says something that I interpret as being inconsistent with the mission of fighting terror, I have a responsibility to point that out. But I don't think it's accurate to say that I'm only portraying them as either fully supportive or completely indifferent. I'm trying to give the American people a clear understanding of where people stand based on what they've actually said.

I thought you were going to ask me about the pig. Well, let's get to the questions. The bombing of Beirut Airport is deeply concerning. It's a tragic reminder of how fragile our world has become. We're working closely with our allies to assess the situation and ensure the safety of civilians. As for the risk of a wider war, I can't ignore the tensions in the region. We're in constant communication with our partners, and we're prepared to take all necessary steps to de-escalate the situation.

Regarding Iran, they've been given time to respond to our concerns, and we're still waiting. We've made it clear that we expect a responsible and transparent response. If they don't come forward, we'll have to consider the implications. But I want to be clear: we're not looking for conflict. We're looking for dialogue and cooperation. The situation is serious, but we remain committed to a peaceful resolution. We're also working with the international community to find a way forward. The world can't afford another war, especially in this volatile region. We'll continue to monitor the situation closely and take action if necessary. But for now, our focus is on de-escalation and ensuring stability.

Thank you for the question. I'm looking forward to hugging everyone when I come back, but I want to be clear—my focus right now is on the work that needs to be done. The country is facing some tough challenges, and I'm committed to getting through them with the strength and unity that this nation deserves. I know that people are eager to see me again, and I share that eagerness. But I also know that the people who are working on the ground, in every corner of this country, need leadership that is steady, focused, and determined. I'm not here to make promises I can't keep, and I'm not here to distract from the real work that needs to be done. I'm here to lead, to listen, and to act. I understand the importance of connection, and I value the trust that people place in me. But I also know that trust is earned through action, not just words. So while I'm happy to see familiar faces and hear familiar voices, I'm also focused on the path ahead. I'm not here to be a distraction, I'm here to be a leader. And when I do come back, I hope it's because I've done the work that this country needs. Until then, I'm here, I'm focused, and I'm committed.

Well, let me be clear: counterfeiting U.S. dollars is a serious issue, and it's something every President has to take seriously. When we catch people trying to counterfeit our currency, we have to act decisively. That's not just about protecting our economy—it's about protecting the integrity of our nation.

Now, regarding the six-party talks, I can tell you that they are a critical part of our strategy in dealing with North Korea. I spoke with President Hu Jintao this morning, and we both recognized the importance of continuing to work together. The six-party talks are not just a diplomatic exercise—they're a way to send a clear message to North Korea that there's a better path than pursuing nuclear weapons. We're not just talking about money laundering; we're talking about the real threat of ballistic missiles and the destabilization they bring to the region.

China has been a key player in these talks, and I believe we need to maintain that collaboration. We have to be united in our approach, because the stakes are too high. North Korea's actions affect not just our country, but the entire region. So yes, we need to stay engaged, and we need to make sure that the six-party talks remain a central part of our strategy.

Mr. Plante, thank you for the question. Let me be clear: this isn't the first time we've discussed these issues, and we've been working closely on both Iran and North Korea. As you know, Russia proposed a very interesting approach to Iran's nuclear program—offering to supply fuel and take back spent fuel. I thought that was a smart, practical solution, and I strongly supported it. It's a way to ensure Iran can have civilian nuclear energy without the risk of proliferation.

On North Korea, we've also been in close coordination. We agree that action at the U.N. is necessary, and we're working to find common language that reflects our shared goals. Our objective is a nuclear-free Korean Peninsula, and we have strong support from Russia, China, Japan, and South Korea. We're focused on diplomacy that is constructive and effective, without undermining the broader negotiations.

As for sanctions, Russia shares our concerns about Iran's nuclear program and is willing to support measures that ensure compliance with international norms. We're committed to working together to achieve a stable, secure world.

Mr. President, I appreciate the question. Let me be clear: we are in constant communication with both Turkey and Iraq on this matter. We have spoken with Ambassador Crocker and General Petraeus this morning, and we are making it very clear to Turkey that we do not believe sending additional troops into Iraq is in their interests. Turkey already has troops stationed in Iraq, and they've had them there for quite some time. We believe that sending more troops—especially in a large-scale, cross-border offensive—would not only be counterproductive but could also escalate tensions in the region.

I want to emphasize that the Iraqi government understands the sensitivity of this issue, which is why Vice President Hashimi is in Istanbul today to engage directly with Turkish leaders. He is there to reassure them that Iraq shares their concerns about terrorist activities, but that there are better ways to address these challenges than sending massive additional troops into the country.

We are actively involved in a tripartite dialogue with Turkey and Iraq, and we will continue to work closely with both nations to find a solution that is stable, secure, and in the best interests of all parties involved.

Well, that's a fair question, and it's one that we're going to have to have a serious conversation about. Let me be clear: I believe in fiscal responsibility, but I also believe in the importance of investing in the things that make our country stronger—like education, infrastructure, and healthcare. If we're talking about making tough choices, we need to make sure we're not cutting the things that are essential for our families and our future. 

Now, if the argument is that we should make deeper spending cuts before considering tax hikes, I think that's a false choice. We can't just cut our way out of this problem. We need a balanced approach that includes both spending reforms and tax policies that are fair and sustainable. 

I know that people want quick fixes, but the reality is that these are complex issues that require thoughtful, long-term solutions. We're going to have to have that adult conversation, and I'm committed to leading that discussion with honesty and transparency. We can't afford to ignore the needs of our families or the long-term health of our economy.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: I have serious concerns about Iran's role in Afghanistan. President Karzai may have expressed optimism, but I remain skeptical. Iran has a history of supporting militant groups and destabilizing the region. They have not proven themselves to be a stabilizing force, and their actions continue to undermine peace and security in Afghanistan. I do not believe they are a positive influence here.

Regarding civilian casualties, I assured President Karzai that we share his concerns and are committed to minimizing harm to innocent lives. Our military operations are conducted with care, and we adjust our tactics to protect civilians whenever possible. However, the Taliban often use civilians as human shields, which makes their actions even more condemnable. We are doing everything we can to ensure that our efforts in Afghanistan are both effective and responsible. I remain focused on protecting the Afghan people and ensuring that the region remains stable and secure.

Thank you for the question. I understand the concern, and I appreciate the scrutiny. But let me be clear — I don't believe we should be judged by the actions of a few, or by the noise that sometimes surrounds them. Our focus has always been on the broader struggle against ideology, against those who would bring violence and terror to our shores and to others. That's the real fight. And yes, we will continue to do what's necessary to protect our people and our values. I've always said that the United States is not perfect, and we will always face criticism. But I also believe that most people around the world still look to us for leadership, for courage, and for a vision of a better future. And that's what we're going to keep working for. So while I won't go into specifics about the CIA tapes, I can say this: we are committed to doing what's right, even when it's hard. And that's what the American people expect of their leaders.

I think, I think—I can't remember his answer; I'm sure you've characterized it perfectly. My attitude is that a young democracy has been born quite quickly. And I think the Iraqi Government has shown remarkable progress on the political front. They developed a modern constitution that was ratified by the people, and then 12 million people voted for a government—which gives me confidence about the future in Iraq, by the way. I hear people say, "Well, civil war this, civil war that." The Iraqi people decided against civil war when they went to the ballot box, and a unity government is working to respond to the will of the people. And frankly, it's quite a remarkable achievement on the political front. The security front is where there have been troubles. It's going to be up to the Maliki Government, with U.S. help, to use the trained forces and eventually a trained police force to take care of those who are trying to foment sectarian violence. We've made some progress against some of those folks, particularly when Mr. Zarqawi met his demise. Remember, Al Qaida is in the country, all attempting to stop the advance of democracy. The blowing up of the mosque created an opportunity for those who were trying to foment sectarian violence to achieve their objective. But the Iraqi people rejected that kind of sectarian violence; the army stood strong. No question, it's still difficult. On the other hand, the political process is part of helping to achieve our objective, which is a free country, an ally in the war on terror that can sustain itself and govern itself and defend itself.

Yes, I am. I believe the American people are smart and they know what they want. They want strong leadership, they want results, and they want to move forward. The Republicans have a clear message, and they've been consistent in their platform. They've worked hard to connect with voters across the country, and I have confidence in their ability to win. The election is still months away, and there's a lot of work to be done. I've been in close contact with my team and with Republican leaders, and we're all focused on making sure we're ready for the challenges ahead. The country is facing a lot of issues—economic uncertainty, inflation, the cost of living, and the need for energy independence. The Republicans have a plan to address these challenges, and I believe they're the best equipped to do so. I also know that the American people are looking for stability and leadership, and I'm confident that the Republicans will deliver. I've seen the enthusiasm in the grassroots, the support from voters, and the strong campaign efforts. We're not just fighting for the House and the Senate—we're fighting for the future of this country. I believe in the strength of the Republican Party, and I'm confident that they will hold both chambers. That's not just my opinion—it's the opinion of the American people who are ready for change and ready for results.

Yes, I do have permission to go inside Pakistan. That's not something I'm going to discuss in detail, but I can tell you that we have the full support of the Pakistani government in our efforts to find and bring to justice those who have attacked our country and our people. We are working closely with them, and that cooperation is essential. We are not here to create problems, but to solve them. We are on the same page, and we are committed to this mission. The President has made it clear that when Usama bin Laden is found, he will be brought to justice. That is our goal, and that is what we are working toward. We are not here to engage in speculation or debate about how it should be done. We are focused on the task at hand, and we are confident in our ability to succeed. Trust and confidence are the foundation of this partnership, and we are committed to maintaining that. We are working together, and we will not let anything stand in the way of justice.

I'm not going to comment on the matter. I've made my position clear, and I'm not going to revisit it. My focus is on moving forward, on the work that needs to be done to unite this country and get things done. I've spent my time in office working on the issues that matter most to the American people—jobs, healthcare, security, and the economy. I don't have time to dwell on speculation or second-guessing. What's important is what we do next. I've always believed in the power of leadership, and that means making decisions that are in the best interest of the nation, not just political convenience. I've been through a lot, and I've learned that the most important thing is to stay focused on the mission. I'm not going to be drawn into this. I've got a lot of work to do, and I need to keep my attention on the people who elected me. Let's talk about the real issues—how we can build a stronger, more prosperous America for all of us.

Thank you for the question. I think it's important to acknowledge that while we've made progress on some fronts—like passing trade agreements and patent reform—our economy still has a long way to go. The recent jobs report showing only 88,000 jobs added is a reminder that we're not moving fast enough. I understand the concerns of my Republican colleagues about the American Jobs Act, particularly the tax provisions. But let me be clear: the tax in question is not on small businesses. It's on high-income individuals—those making over a million dollars a year. And as I've said, less than 3 percent of small businesses even reach that level. So when they say they don't want to tax small businesses, they're not being honest with themselves or with the American people.

I believe I've been an effective leader on the economy. When I took office, the economy was in a deep recession, and we've since seen steady growth. But we can do better. I'm not asking for a political compromise that hurts the middle class or small businesses. I'm asking for common sense solutions that create jobs, rebuild infrastructure, and put people back to work. If Congress is willing to set aside partisan gridlock and work with me, I'm ready to move forward. But until then, we'll continue to take administrative steps to support the economy. The time for action is now.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: North Korea has been pursuing nuclear weapons for a long time, long before I came into office. It's a threat we've taken seriously, and we continue to do so. In 1994, the U.S. entered into a bilateral agreement with North Korea to ensure they wouldn't develop nuclear weapons. But when we came into office, we discovered they were secretly advancing a program, which they had agreed not to do. We confronted them, and they admitted it. Then they walked away from the agreement.

Since then, we've tried again, bringing other nations to the table in the six-party talks. North Korea agreed to verifiably show they weren't developing weapons, but again, they walked away. The problem isn't the U.S. policy—it's the intransigence of the North Korean leader. He refuses to choose a better path for his country.

Some say the U.S. should go it alone with North Korea, but that didn't work before. The lesson learned is that a stronger diplomatic hand comes from working with allies who share the same goal: a nuclear-free peninsula. That's why we've chosen a multilateral approach. It's not about blame—it's about strategy. And we're committed to finding a diplomatic solution.

No, Deb, I think people who are saying we're moving forward to a full war are wrong. What we're doing is not a full war. We're supporting the Maliki Government in their efforts to stabilize the country and bring about a democratic system. This is a long-term strategy, not a short-term military campaign. We're helping them deal with the violence that's been fomented by extremist groups, including Al Qaida, which seeks to undermine the emergence of a democracy in Iraq. A democracy in the heart of the Middle East is not just important for Iraq—it's vital for the entire region. It's a way to counter the spread of radical ideologies and to promote peace and stability. The people of Iraq have shown through their votes that they want a Constitution, a government that reflects their will, and a future where they can live in peace. Our role is to support that process, not to impose a war. We're working with the Maliki Government to help them succeed, and that's in our mutual interest. The extremists are trying to stop this, but the people of Iraq are determined. And that's why we're here.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are critical to our housing market, but they need to be reformed. Our administration has proposed a robust reform package that will ensure they focus on their core mission—supporting home ownership through stable, affordable mortgages. That means they should not be allowed to expand beyond their current limits or take on additional roles that could destabilize the system. We need to bring regulatory oversight in line with other lending institutions, so they operate with the same level of accountability and transparency. First things first—Congress needs to get these institutions reformed, streamlined, and focused. Only then can we consider other options to help revive mortgage finance. The key is to ensure that the housing market is stable, predictable, and accessible for all Americans. We can't afford to repeat the mistakes of the past. So while we're working on reform, we're not looking to expand their role in ways that could create new risks. Let's get this right, and then we can move forward with confidence.

A competitive dollar is absolutely essential to keeping U.S. exports strong and growing. When the dollar is strong, it makes our exports more expensive for foreign buyers, which can hurt our competitiveness in global markets. That's why we're committed to a strong dollar policy. A strong dollar reflects the strength of our economy, and that strength is what allows us to maintain a competitive edge in the global marketplace. We believe that a strong economy with solid fundamentals—like low inflation, strong employment, and sustainable growth—will naturally support a strong dollar. And a strong dollar, in turn, helps maintain the confidence of our trading partners and investors. We're not looking to weaken the dollar for short-term gains; we're focused on long-term economic stability and growth. Our goal is to ensure that the U.S. remains a leader in the global economy, and a strong dollar is a key part of that strategy. We're confident that with the right policies in place, our economy will continue to grow, and the dollar will remain strong and resilient.

I'm not sure I'd call it frustration. It's more like a deep sense of responsibility. These are difficult times, and I know that people are feeling the weight of it. Nobody wants to see innocent lives lost, and I share that pain. Every day, we're reminded of the cost of conflict, and it's hard not to feel the strain on our country's spirit. But I also believe in the power of our nation to rise to these challenges. We've faced tough moments before, and we've always found a way forward. The question is whether we have the will and the capacity to stand up to those who would bring harm and to support those who seek freedom. That's what this moment demands. We must act with strength, but also with compassion. We must show the world that we are not just a nation of power, but of purpose. And I believe we have that purpose. We owe it to our children, and to the people who are suffering, to do everything in our power to bring peace. That's not just a goal—it's a promise.

If so, why? And do you believe that the biggest drag on the Republican Party is the situation in Iraq?

Well, Bret, the situation in Iraq is certainly a tough issue for the American people, and it's a serious one. But I don't think it's the biggest drag on the Republican Party. The biggest issues in this campaign are the economy and national security. The economy is growing, unemployment is at 4.6 percent, and we've added 6.6 million jobs since 2003. Gas prices are down, and tax cuts are working. The Democrats, on the other hand, want to raise taxes, and I believe that's just a code word for raising taxes on whoever they can. 

On the security front, the American people know we have to protect this country from further attacks. We've seen the threat is real, and we've taken action to stop it. The Democrats, however, have shown a different view of the world. They've voted against programs that help us fight terror, like interrogating high-value detainees or listening in on Al Qaida communications. I don't question their patriotism, but I do question their strategy. We can't wait for an attack to respond. We must defeat the enemy overseas so we don't have to face them here. Iraq is part of the war on terror, and I believe the American people know that.

No, I’m not saying that. The NIE reaffirms what we’ve been saying all along—that the situation with Iran is dangerous, and that the policies we’ve been pursuing to deter them are still the right ones. The report isn’t a signal to ease up or take a backseat. It’s a reminder that the risks are real, and that the tools we’ve used in the past—like sanctions, diplomatic pressure, and support for regional allies—are still effective. The challenge is that convincing the private sector to support these efforts is harder than getting governments to speak out. Many companies are worried about losing market share or facing economic risks. So, I’ve been working closely with my counterparts to show them that this isn’t just about politics—it’s about long-term stability and peace. The U.S. policy remains firm: we see a danger, and we’re committed to working with the world to ensure that Iran doesn’t repeat the mistakes of the past. That means continuing the pressure, but also finding ways to make it in the interest of everyone involved. The hard work is ahead, but it’s necessary.

I certainly hope so. In order for the U.N. to be effective, there must be consequences if people thumb their nose at the United Nations Security Council. And we will work with people in the Security Council to achieve that objective, and the objective is that there's got to be a consequence for them basically ignoring what the Security Council has suggested through resolution. We are all aware of the importance of maintaining international order and ensuring that nations comply with collective decisions. The Security Council has a responsibility to act decisively when necessary, and we are prepared to support that effort. The situation with Iran is a clear example of why the U.N. must remain a strong and unified body. We cannot allow one nation to act unilaterally and undermine the collective will of the international community. If Iran continues down this path, then the Security Council must be ready to impose meaningful sanctions. We are confident that the Council will move quickly and decisively if needed. Our commitment is to uphold the principles of the U.N. and ensure that all members respect the resolutions passed by the Council. This is not just about Iran—it's about the credibility and effectiveness of the entire international system.

I think it's safe to say that sometime next year, we'll be able to have that meeting. I've been in communication with the North Korean leadership, and we're working toward a time when we can sit down and talk directly. It's important that we continue to engage with North Korea in a way that promotes stability and denuclearization. I believe that dialogue is the best path forward, and I remain committed to that approach. While the exact timing is still being worked out, I'm confident that we're moving in the right direction. The goal is to create a framework for peace and security on the Korean Peninsula, and I'm working closely with my team and our allies to make that a reality. I understand the importance of patience and consistency in these matters, and I'm prepared to do what it takes to ensure that the process is both meaningful and productive. I also want to emphasize that any meeting will be based on mutual respect and the shared objective of reducing tensions. I'm hopeful that we can achieve this in the coming months, and I look forward to sharing more details as the situation develops.

Thank you for the question. I am certainly aware of the Occupy Wall Street movement and the broader frustrations that it represents. I've seen the protests on television, and I understand the anger and disillusionment that many people feel. The American people have endured a financial crisis that affected them in real and painful ways—job losses, home foreclosures, and a sense that the system is rigged against them. And yet, in many cases, the same individuals and institutions that contributed to the crisis are still in power, and in some cases, even more powerful.

I believe that the frustrations of the American people are valid, and I think the movement is giving voice to those frustrations. But I also believe that we need a strong, stable financial system to grow our economy. That’s why I fought so hard to pass Dodd-Frank. It was a difficult and politically costly decision, but it was necessary to prevent another financial collapse and to protect the American people from the same mistakes that got us into this mess in the first place.

We need to ensure that banks and financial institutions compete on the basis of fair practices, not hidden fees or deceptive tactics. That’s what Dodd-Frank was designed to do. And that’s why I’m committed to defending those reforms, even when it means standing up to those who want to roll them back. The American people deserve a financial system that works for them, not just for the few.

Mr. President, I would react with the same clarity and firmness that I expect from our own service members. If an American were captured and treated in a manner that violated the laws we uphold, regardless of where that occurred, we would hold those responsible accountable. The Geneva Conventions are not a suggestion—they are a standard. But the problem is, the standards we have now are too vague, too open to interpretation. That’s why we need clear, enforceable laws. If we don’t, we risk sending a message that our own people can be treated with impunity. And that’s not acceptable. Our soldiers, our intelligence officers, they are not going to break the law, no matter how difficult the situation. They are not going to be told, “Do what you have to do, and we won’t prosecute you.” That’s not how we run this country. We have a duty to protect our people, but we also have a duty to uphold the law. That’s why this debate is so important. It’s not just about interrogation—it’s about the values we stand for.

No, I don't think that's fair. What I've said is clear: I'm focused on achieving our objectives in Iraq, not on setting arbitrary timelines or dates for withdrawal. The decision to adjust troop levels will be based on the progress we're seeing on the ground—specifically, the improvement in security conditions. General Petraeus and Ambassador Crocker are returning to provide their assessment, and I will take their recommendations into account as I develop the strategy moving forward. I've been candid about this, both on Air Force One and in Baghdad. If the situation continues to improve, we may be able to achieve our goals with fewer troops. But until we have the full report from the generals, I won't make any final decisions. My priority is ensuring that we are successful in Iraq, and that means being flexible and responsive to the situation as it evolves. I'm not trying to appease anyone—I'm trying to lead with clarity and purpose.

My point was that bilateral negotiations didn't work. I appreciate the efforts of previous administrations, but they just didn't lead to a solution. So I thought it was important to change how we approached the problem so that we could solve it diplomatically. I firmly believe that with North Korea and with Iran, it's best to deal with these regimes with more than one voice, because I understand how it works. What ends up happening is, we say to a country like North Korea, "Here's a reasonable way forward." They try to extract more at the negotiating table, or they have a different objective, and then they go and say, "Wait a minute; the United States is being unreasonable." They make a threat. They could say the world is about to fall apart because of the United States problem. And all of a sudden, we become the issue.

But the United States message to North Korea and Iran is that we want to solve issues peacefully. We said there's a better way forward for you. Here's a chance, for example, to help your country economically. And all you got to do is verifiably show that you—in Iran's case, that you suspended your weapons program, and in North Korea's case, that you've got international safeguards on your program—which they agreed to, by the way.

My point is that to the American people, I say, look, we want to solve this diplomatically. It's important for the President to say to the American people, diplomacy was our first choice, and that I've now outlined a strategy. And it's a hopeful sign that China is now an integral partner in helping North Korea understand that it's not just the United States speaking to them. It's an important sign to North Korea that South Korea, a country deeply concerned about North Korean activities, is a partner. No, I don’t regret the decision. I made it based on the information I had at the time, and I believed that a diplomatic approach was the best path forward. I’ve always been clear that we have a responsibility to pursue peace and stability in the region, and that requires patience, persistence, and partnership. I’ve worked closely with our allies—China, South Korea, Japan, and Russia—to build a unified front. I made it clear that we are not looking for confrontation, but rather a way to bring North Korea into the fold through dialogue and mutual respect. I also reconfirmed our security commitments to our allies, because that’s part of the equation. I understand the frustration when diplomacy seems to stall, but I believe in the long game. I’ve always said that the best way to deal with a problem is to address it head-on, not through force or coercion. I remain committed to finding a diplomatic solution, and I will continue to work with our partners to make that happen. That’s what I owe the American people.

Thank you for the question. I believe that being a moral leader is about doing what's right for the American people, not just what's popular or politically convenient. I've always believed in leading with integrity, and I think that's what people see when they look at my record. I've worked across the aisle, and I've made it a priority to find common ground. That's not just about politics—it's about the country. I've had some tough conversations, but I believe in the power of dialogue. I think the American people deserve leaders who are willing to put the nation first, even when it's hard. I've seen firsthand how division can hurt us, and I've also seen how unity can bring us together. I'm not afraid to take on difficult issues, and I'm not afraid to admit when I'm wrong. That's part of being a moral leader. I believe in the values that this country was founded on—freedom, equality, and opportunity. And I believe that those values are worth fighting for. I'm proud to be the President of the United States, and I'm committed to leading with honesty and compassion. I know there's a lot of work to be done, but I'm confident that with hard work and a shared vision, we can make this country even better.

He poses a unique set of challenges, Jim, but I think the key is to understand that he lives in a very closed society, where there's no press, no open dialogue, and no transparency. We don't know what he's thinking, and that's the problem. We do know, however, that there are concentration camps, that people are starving, and that our nation has tried to help feed the hungry. But we don't know his intentions, and that's why we have to plan for the worst and hope for the best.

One of the biggest threats we face is the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. That's why we have the Proliferation Security Initiative, and why we work closely with allies and the six-party talks. We want to encourage diplomacy, but we also want to make sure that we're not allowing any threat to come home to hurt the American people. The lesson of September 11th is that we're vulnerable, and we can't take that risk again. We're not looking to confront him, but we are looking to make sure that he knows that we're not going to allow him to threaten us. We're working with our allies, and we're sending a clear message. That's the way to deal with threats diplomatically.
